samples.prompt: Write three short anecdotal examples illustrating how unconventional or eccentric behavior can be more persuasive than eloquent rhetoric.
samples.generated: It is not uncommon for people to make decisions based on an unusual piece of clothing, a strange accent, or some other odd characteristic. For example, I remember one time that I went to a meeting where it was raining outside. The only person who came in with umbrellas was me because I had taken them home from my last trip. At that meeting we were discussing whether to build another road into town. The man who spoke next said something like, "The way to get this road built is by building bridges." Everyone laughed at him until he made up his mind to stop laughing and listen to what he was saying. Then he became very persuasive. He did not mention any statistics. He used a picture to prove his point. When he finished talking, there was no doubt in anyone’s mind. I have also known two women whose husbands died within a month of each other. One had a habit of going to bed very late; the other would go out and spend all her money if she could. Both of these habits brought her back together again.

I was born in San Francisco (my mother is an artist), raised in Oakland (a city where everyone knows each other) until I was 12. Then I went up to Berkeley to live with my grandparents. Now I'm back again in San Francisco, working at a law firm.
For a long time there were no places near here that I missed very much. We have read of some celebrated philosopher who was so absent-minded
that he paid a call at his own house. My own absent-mindedness is
extreme, and my philosophy, of course, is the marvel of men and angels.
But I never quite managed to be so absent-minded as that. Some yards at
least from my own door, something vaguely familiar has always caught
my eye; and thus the joke has been spoiled. Of course I have quite
constantly walked into another man's house, thinking it was my own
house; my visits became almost monotonous. But walking into my own house
and thinking it was another man's house is a flight of poetic detachment
still beyond me. Something of the sensations that such an absent-minded
man must feel I really felt the other day; and very pleasant sensations
they were. The best parts of every proper romance are the first chapter
and the last chapter; and to knock at a strange door and find a nice
wife would be to concentrate the beginning and end of all romance.
